lead: A skew load on a section with unequal principal second moments bends the beam in two planes at once. Each plane obeys the ordinary beam formula, so you integrate twice about each principal axis and get two deflection components. The real movement is their vector sum. The tip does not follow the load line: it swings towards the more flexible plane. Designers use this to check that a spar tip, a strut or a control-surface hinge does not move where the drawing assumed. It is the deflection half of the unsymmetrical bending problem whose stresses are in Chapter 4.2.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for the neutral axis and the two-plane split of stress, and the beam deflection formulas of Unit 2.

blocks.text: Take u and v as the principal centroidal axes of the cross-section. The product second moment I_uv is zero, so bending in the u–z plane and bending in the v–z plane do not interact: a moment in one plane produces no curvature in the other. That is what turns the deflection problem into two easy beam problems.

blocks.where: 1/R_u is the curvature of the beam axis in the u–z plane (1/m); M_u is the moment bending the beam in that plane (N·m); E is Young's modulus (Pa); I_u is the second moment of area of the section for bending in the u–z plane (m⁴).
1/R_v is the curvature in the v–z plane (1/m); M_v is the moment in that plane (N·m); I_v is the second moment of area for bending in the v–z plane (m⁴).

blocks.text: Label convention: I_u is the second moment about the v axis, I_u = ∫u² dA, the value used in σ = M u / I_u for bending in the u–z plane; I_v = ∫v² dA is about the u axis. Some books swap these labels; check which one the formula is written with.

Curvature is the rate at which the slope changes along the span. The deflection components u(z) and v(z) therefore come from two ordinary integrations, d²u/dz² = M_u/(E I_u) and d²v/dz² = M_v/(E I_v), with the sign convention of Unit 2. The constants are fixed by the supports: slope and deflection are zero at a fixed end, deflection is zero at a simple support.

For common loads, skip the integration. Resolve the load into the two planes, take the closed-form deflection for each plane from Unit 2, and combine at the end. Integrate only for loads that are not in the table.

sections.h3: Cantilever with a skew tip load

items: Resolve the tip load P acting at angle θ from the u-axis: P_u = P cos θ along u and P_v = P sin θ along v.
Take the cantilever formula in each plane: δ_u = P_u L³/(3 E I_u) and δ_v = P_v L³/(3 E I_v).
Combine the two as vectors: δ = √(δ_u² + δ_v²), at angle β = tan⁻¹(δ_v/δ_u) from the u-axis.
Compare β with θ. The two angles are equal only when I_u = I_v.

blocks.where: δ_u is the tip deflection in the u direction (m); P_u is the load component along u (N); L is the span (m); E is Young's modulus (Pa); I_u is the second moment for bending in the u–z plane (m⁴).

blocks.text: The direction comes from dividing one component by the other: tan β = δ_v/δ_u = tan θ × (I_u/I_v). When the v-plane is the more flexible one, I_v < I_u, so I_u/I_v > 1 and β > θ; the tip swings away from the load line towards v. The tip also lies at right angles to the neutral axis of Chapter 4.2, so the movement and the zero-stress line are perpendicular.

Both components share the same shape along the span, δ_u(z) = δ_u z²(3L − z)/(2L³), and the v component has the same form. The whole elastic curve therefore lies in one plane at angle β, and every station moves in that direction. Small-deflection theory is assumed: β stays fixed as the load grows.

Other supports change the coefficient and the shape in each plane, but both planes still share the same shape, so you resolve, take the tabulated deflection in each plane, and combine as vectors. A simply supported span L with a central load P at angle θ gives δ_u = P_u L³/(48 E I_u) and δ_v = P_v L³/(48 E I_v). A uniform load w N/m gives 5wL⁴/(384 E I) in each plane.

Two checks catch most errors. The resultant must lie between the larger component and the plain sum of the components. The direction must lie between θ and the flexible axis, and on the load line only for a section with I_u = I_v, such as a square or circular tube.

On an aircraft the direction matters as much as the size. A spar tip that moves at 72° while the lift acts at 37° opens or closes the gap at a control-surface hinge and misaligns bolted fittings. Unit 6 carries that direction into aeroelastic calculations.

figure.caption: The two components of the 2 m cantilever of the worked example: the u-plane curve reaches 7.6 mm and the v-plane curve reaches 22.9 mm at the tip, so the tip movement lies much nearer the v direction than the load does.

spec.aria: Two deflection curves for the same cantilever: the component in the u–z plane grows to 7.62 mm and the component in the v–z plane grows to 22.86 mm, so the flexible-plane component dominates the tip movement.

examples.question: A thin-walled aluminium cantilever has length L = 2 m, E = 70 GPa, and principal second moments I_u = 4 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and I_v = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ for bending in the u–z and v–z planes. A tip load P = 1 kN acts at 36.87° from the u-axis (the 3-4-5 angle). Find the tip deflection in each plane, the resultant deflection and its direction, and compare with the load direction.
steps: Convert to base units: E = 70 GPa = 70 × 10⁹ N/m², P = 1000 N, L³ = 2³ = 8 m³.
Direction: β = tan⁻¹(22.86 / 7.62) = tan⁻¹(3.00) = 71.6° from the u-axis.
Compare: the load is at 36.9° but the tip moves at 71.6°, a swing of 34.7° towards the flexible v-plane, so the tip is not on the load line.
examples.answer: δ_u = 7.6 mm, δ_v = 22.9 mm, resultant 24.1 mm at 71.6° from the u-axis, while the load acts at 36.9°.
examples.check:
import math
L = 2.0
E = 70e9
Iu = 4e-6
Iv = 1e-6
P = 1000.0
th = math.atan2(600.0, 800.0)
Pu = P*math.cos(th)
Pv = P*math.sin(th)
du = Pu*L**3/(3*E*Iu)
dv = Pv*L**3/(3*E*Iv)
d = math.hypot(du, dv)
beta = math.degrees(math.atan2(dv, du))
print(f"{Pu:.1f}")
print(f"{Pv:.1f}")
print(f"{du*1000:.1f}")
print(f"{dv*1000:.1f}")
print(f"{d*1000:.1f}")
print(f"{beta:.1f}")

traps: Adding the components as plain numbers: 7.6 + 22.9 = 30.5 mm is wrong; the vector sum is 24.1 mm.
Drawing the tip deflection along the load line. A skew load on unequal second moments always lands nearer the flexible plane.
Pairing a deflection component with the wrong second moment. Each component uses the second moment for its own bending plane, which is the value about the axis perpendicular to that plane.
Unit slips: I in mm⁴ with E in GPa. Convert first, since 1 mm⁴ = 10⁻¹² m⁴, and keep L in metres.
Using cos θ on the wrong component: the cosine multiplies the component along the axis from which θ is measured.

quiz.q: State the curvature relation for bending in the u–z plane and define every symbol.
quiz.a: 1/R_u = M_u/(E I_u), with 1/R_u the curvature in the u–z plane (1/m), M_u the moment in that plane (N·m), E Young's modulus (Pa) and I_u the second moment of area for that plane (m⁴).

quiz.q: Why does the two-plane split fail when the axes are not principal?
quiz.a: With I_uv ≠ 0 the planes are coupled: a moment in one plane also produces curvature in the other, so two separate integrations no longer describe the beam and the full unsymmetrical equations of Chapter 4.2 are needed.

quiz.q: A cantilever has L = 1.5 m, E = 200 GPa, I_u = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, I_v = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. A tip load of 500 N acts at 30° from the u-axis. Find the tip deflection components and the resultant.
A lift load acts at 20° from the u-axis, but the spar tip moves at 60°. What does this say about the section?
quiz.a: tan β/tan θ = I_u/I_v = tan 60°/tan 20° = 1.73/0.364 ≈ 4.8. The v-plane is about 4.8 times more flexible than the u-plane, so the section is deep along u and thin along v, and the tip swings towards v.

quiz.q: Both deflection components share the shape z²(3L − z). What does that imply about the elastic curve?
quiz.a: The curve lies in a single plane at angle β, and every station along the span moves in that same direction; bending alone introduces no twist.

quiz.q: A square tube has I_u = I_v. Where does the tip of a cantilever move under a skew tip load?
quiz.a: Along the load line: tan β = tan θ × (I_u/I_v) = tan θ, so β = θ and there is no off-axis movement.

quiz.q: Write the resultant tip deflection and its direction for a cantilever under a skew tip load.
quiz.a: δ = √(δ_u² + δ_v²) and β = tan⁻¹(δ_v/δ_u) measured from the u-axis, with δ_u = P_u L³/(3EI_u) and δ_v = P_v L³/(3EI_v).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same split is written as a 2 × 2 flexibility matrix, and for a composite wing the bending–twisting coupling of the laminate adds off-diagonal terms, so a load can twist the section as well as bend it. Aeroelastic tools combine this deflection direction with the aerodynamic centre to predict divergence and loss of control effectiveness. A short plotting exercise along the span, in MATLAB or Python, shows how the tip direction is set by the second-moment ratio and not by the load. Search for 'unsymmetrical bending principal axes deflection', 'bending–twisting coupling composite beam' and 'aeroelastic divergence wing'.
